name: Transient osteoporosis of the hip
aliases: transient bone marrow oedema of the hip

clinicalPearls: A self-limiting cause of hip pain characterised by transient bone marrow oedema and reversible osteopenia
Classically affects middle-aged men and women in the third trimester of pregnancy
Presents with progressive hip pain and limp without preceding trauma
Radiographs show osteopenia of the femoral head after some weeks, while MRI shows marrow oedema without the necrosis of avascular necrosis
It is considered part of the bone marrow oedema syndrome spectrum and is a key differential of early avascular necrosis
It resolves spontaneously over months with protected weight bearing and analgesia
reference.pathophysiology: Transient osteoporosis of the hip is characterised by self-limiting bone marrow oedema of the femoral head and neck with associated localised, reversible bone loss. The cause is uncertain; proposed mechanisms include transient ischaemia, altered local blood flow or a neurovascular response, and in pregnancy mechanical and hormonal factors may contribute. Unlike avascular necrosis, there is no established osteonecrosis, and the oedema and osteopenia resolve completely, distinguishing it on MRI and by its benign natural history.
additionalDifferentials: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
additionalInvestigations: MRI showing bone marrow oedema without necrosis
Assessment for pregnancy and osteoporosis risk factors
redFlags: Features suggesting septic arthritis or osteomyelitis
Imaging evidence of established avascular necrosis or subchondral collapse
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting, typically resolving over six to twelve months with conservative management and no long-term sequelae.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for avascular necrosis and intervening unnecessarily
Overlooking infection when there are systemic features
Failing to protect the hip, risking fracture during the osteopenic phase
management: Protected weight-bearing with crutches or a walking aid to offload the femoral head and reduce fracture risk while the marrow oedema resolves
Analgesia for pain control during the symptomatic phase
Consider bisphosphonate therapy with calcium and vitamin D repletion to hasten resolution of the bone marrow oedema in selected cases
Physiotherapy to preserve hip range of movement and muscle strength while weight-bearing is restricted
Serial MRI follow-up to confirm resolution and to distinguish the condition from evolving avascular necrosis
In pregnancy-associated disease, coordinate analgesia and mobility support with obstetric care, expecting spontaneous resolution after delivery
